messages.content:
You are a clinical psychologist writing a psychological case vignette
grounded in Ehlers & Clark's (2000) cognitive model of PTSD.

Write a realistic clinical case vignette for a patient with PTSD.
The vignette should read as a cohesive, flowing portrait — not a structured report.
Weave together who this person is, what happened to them, how they experience their
symptoms day to day, how they cope, and what toll this takes on their life and relationships.


Do not use section headers, numbered points, or clinical labels for symptoms.
Write 200–300 words in third person.
Cover: presenting complaints, trauma background, cognitive distortions, avoidance, and maintaining factors.
Avoid excessive jargon - write for a clinical case conference audience.

Please write a clinical vignette for the following patient presenting with PTSD.
Patient demographics:
- Age: 52
- Gender: Male
- Ethnicity: European
- Relationship Status: In a relationship
- Occupation: Film Director
- Trauma Type: Life-threatening accident
- Pcl5: 35

Elias sits across from me, his posture rigid in the armchair, hands resting flat on his knees. At fifty-two, he carries the quiet authority of a man who once directed films across European festival circuits, but now that authority feels hollow. He works on independent documentaries, a craft that once demands he orchestrate chaos into coherent narratives. Lately, he tells me, he can only imagine scenes in reverse, watching them fracture before they ever begin. Six months ago, on a rain-slicked coastal highway, a delivery truck hydroplanes into his lane. Elias remembers the glass blooming across his windshield like frost, the sickening lurch of metal folding inward, and the sudden, impossible silence that follows when his car finally rests upside down in the ditch. He crawls out through the shattered passenger window, lungs burning with antifreeze and damp earth. Paramedics find him sitting in the tall grass three miles from the crash site, shivering, insisting he is fine while his left leg hangs at a wrong angle. The accident does not end at the roadside. It follows him home. Now, Elias avoids highways entirely, taking winding backroads that add forty minutes to every commute. He tells me he stops filming. When his production team calls to discuss a new grant proposal, he lets the phone ring, then calls back with a flat excuse about creative differences. In the editing suite, where he once thrives on pacing and rhythm, the whir of the projector and the staccato click of a clapperboard trigger a sudden tightness in his chest. He has taken to wearing noise-canceling headphones on set, claiming they help him focus, but I notice how his shoulders jump when a crew member drops a cable. His partner, Clara, tries to hold space for the changes. She leaves his favorite coffee on the desk, asks gentle questions about the days he wakes before dawn, and waits in the passenger seat during errands. But Elias admits he no longer sleeps beside her. When she reaches for his hand in the dark, his body tenses, and he finds himself mentally drafting the next day’s shot list just to keep his thoughts from drifting backward. He watches her sleep sometimes, feeling a heavy, unnameable distance settle between them, as though he has seen too many endings to trust the next beginning. On screen, Elias describes how the trauma rewires his perception. A sudden brake light on a city street sends his pulse hammering against his ribs. He catches himself counting exits in every restaurant, mapping evacuation routes in the back of his mind while the waiter waits with a menu. At night, his sleep fractures. He wakes at 3 a.m. with the taste of copper and diesel on his tongue, convinced the ceiling is tilting. He gets up, checks the car keys in his bag twice, and watches the streetlights through the blinds until the gray light of morning. He tells me he misses the old version of himself—the one who could sit in a dark theater and let a story unfold without analyzing every shadow. Now, in our sessions, Elias speaks in measured tones, tracing the contours of what he lost with a director’s precision. He notices how his breath quickens when I mention the word “car.” He admits he no longer dreams of the crash; instead, he dreams of standing on a soundstage that keeps shrinking until he must choose which wall to run through. He leaves my office every Tuesday with his coat buttoned tightly, scanning the traffic at the corner, already bracing for the next scene.
